topic_title: Judiciary in India: Supreme Court, High Courts, Judicial Review, PIL & Emergency Provisions
syllabus_mapping: Judiciary in India - Structure and functions, important provisions relating to emergency and constitutional amendments, judicial review, Public Interest Litigation.

content.text: The Indian Judicial Architecture: Integrated Courts, Judicial Review, PIL, and Emergency Provisions

Unlike the dual court system of the United States, India possesses an integrated and unified judicial hierarchy headed by the Supreme Court of India (Articles 124 to 147), followed by High Courts in the States (Articles 214 to 231) and Subordinate Courts. The judiciary acts as the guardian of the Constitution, protector of Fundamental Rights, and final arbiter of federal disputes under the powers of Judicial Review and Public Interest Litigation (PIL).
1. Structure, Jurisdictions & Powers of the Supreme Court

content.caption: Constitutional Jurisdictions of the Supreme Court of India
rows: Exclusive original jurisdiction in inter-governmental disputes: (1) Centre vs. One or more States; (2) Centre and State(s) vs. State(s); (3) Between two or more States. Excludes pre-constitution treaties and inter-state river water disputes (Art. 262).

Direct enforcement of Fundamental Rights; issues prerogative writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo-Warranto). Concurrent with High Courts under Article 226 (High Court writ jurisdiction is wider, extending to legal rights as well).
Constitutional matters (substantial question of law), Civil appeals, and Criminal appeals against High Court judgments certified under Article 134A.
Plenary discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal against any judgment, decree, or sentence of any court or tribunal in India (except military tribunals).
President may seek SC opinion on questions of public law or fact (non-binding advisory opinion, e.g., Delhi Laws Act, Berubari, Re: Special Courts Bill).
Art. 129: Power to punish for contempt of itself. Art. 142: Inherent power to pass any decree or order necessary for doing 'complete justice' in any cause or matter.

content.text: 2. High Court of Andhra Pradesh & Subordinate Judiciary

Following the 2014 bifurcation, the High Court of Judicature at Hyderabad served as the common high court until the separate High Court of Andhra Pradesh was constituted on January 1, 2019, by Presidential Order under the AP Reorganisation Act 2014, operating from its seat at Nelapadu, Amaravati:

items: Writ Powers (Article 226): High Courts enjoy wider territorial and subject-matter writ jurisdiction than the Supreme Court, capable of issuing writs for Fundamental Rights and 'for any other purpose' (ordinary legal rights).

Superintendence over Subordinate Courts (Article 227): Administrative and judicial superintendence over all district courts, sessions courts, family courts, and tribunals within the state's territory.

Subordinate Judiciary (Articles 233–237): District Judges appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court. Civil hierarchy: District Court -> Senior Civil Judge -> Junior Civil Judge; Criminal hierarchy: Sessions Court -> Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) -> Judicial Magistrate First Class (JMFC).

content.text: 3. Judicial Appointments: The Collegium System vs. NJAC
The mechanism for appointing judges to higher courts evolved through the landmark 'Three Judges Cases':

content.caption: Evolution of the Higher Judicial Appointment Mechanism in India
rows: First Judges Case (SP Gupta v. UOI, 1981)
Held that 'consultation' does not mean 'concurrence' under Articles 124(2) and 217(1); the executive holds final primacy in judicial appointments.
Overruled SP Gupta; ruled that 'consultation' means 'concurrence'; institutionalized the Collegium (CJI + two senior-most SC judges) to maintain judicial independence.
Expanded Collegium to CJI + four senior-most judges for Supreme Court appointments, and CJI + two senior-most judges for High Court transfers.

Supreme Court by 4:1 majority struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act and the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act, holding that judicial primacy in appointments forms an unamendable core of the Basic Structure.

content.text: 4. Judicial Review, Judicial Activism, and Public Interest Litigation (PIL)

Judicial Review is the power of courts to examine the constitutional validity of legislative enactments and executive orders (grounded in Articles 13, 32, 136, 226). In India, judicial review evolved into proactive Judicial Activism through Public Interest Litigation (PIL):

items: Genesis of PIL: Pioneered in the late 1970s and 1980s by Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer (e.g., Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary Bihar 1979 for undertrial prisoners; S.P. Gupta 1981).

Relaxation of Locus Standi: Any public-spirited individual or citizen group can move the court on behalf of disadvantaged, impoverished, or marginalized citizens who cannot approach the court themselves.
Epistolary Jurisdiction: Courts treat simple letters, postcards, or newspaper reports as writ petitions.

Judicial Overreach Dilemma: Concerns arise when courts stray into policy formulation, budgetary allocations, or administrative execution (e.g., framing vehicular emission norms, liquor bans on highways, restructuring sports administration), potentially disturbing the separation of powers under Article 50.

content.caption: The Three Types of Constitutional Emergencies in India
rows: War, External Aggression, or 'Armed Rebellion' (substituted for 'internal disturbance' by 44th Amendment 1978).

Requires written recommendation of Union Cabinet; approved by special majority of both Houses within 1 month; valid for 6 months at a time. Art. 19 automatically suspended under Art. 358 only for war/external aggression; Articles 20 and 21 CANNOT be suspended even during emergency (44th Amendment).
Failure of constitutional machinery in a State (Art. 356) or failure to comply with Union executive directions (Art. 365).
Approved by simple majority within 2 months; maximum duration 3 years (with conditions after 1 year under Art. 356(5)); subject to judicial review under S.R. Bommai (1994).
Threat to financial stability or credit of India or any part thereof.
Approved by simple majority within 2 months; indefinite duration until revoked; President can direct reduction of salaries of public servants including SC/HC judges. Never declared in India.

content.text: Part A: Mains Analytical & Descriptive Questions

items:
Explain the origin, philosophical foundations, and procedural mechanics of Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India. Distinguish between legitimate Judicial Activism and Judicial Overreach. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Define PIL as a revolutionary procedural innovation expanding justice access (Justices Krishna Iyer & P.N. Bhagwati); detail procedural departures (relaxation of strict locus standi, epistolary jurisdiction, appointing amicus curiae/fact-finding commissions); examine positive transformations (bonded labor abolition, prison reforms, environmental protection via M.C. Mehta cases); analyze the fine distinction between Judicial Activism (filling legislative vacuums in human rights protection) and Judicial Overreach (entering core executive/legislative domains like fiscal policy, administrative staffing, or policy micro-management); conclude with guidelines to check frivolous, publicity-oriented PILs.

Critically evaluate the debate between the Collegium System of judicial appointments and the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC). How can transparency and meritocracy be harmonized with judicial independence? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Trace evolution of the Collegium through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998); examine the rationale of the 99th Amendment Act 2014 creating the NJAC (balancing executive, civil society, and judicial inputs); analyze the Supreme Court's 2015 verdict striking down NJAC as violating the Basic Structure (judicial primacy in appointments as essential to independence); outline persistent criticisms of the Collegium (nepotism, opacity, lack of institutional criteria, delay in filling vacancies); suggest structural reforms: institutionalizing a formal Secretariat, objective eligibility criteria, and a revised Memorandum of Procedure (MoP).

Discuss the impact of the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 on the Emergency Provisions of the Indian Constitution. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Frame the context of the 1975–77 Internal Emergency excesses; enumerate key safeguards introduced by the 44th Amendment: (1) Replacing subjective 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' in Article 352; (2) Mandating written advice of the Union Cabinet before proclamation; (3) Raising parliamentary approval majority from simple to special majority within 1 month; (4) Making periodic review mandatory every 6 months; (5) Ensuring Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended during any emergency, overcoming the tragic precedent of ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976).

content.text: Part B: Screening / Prelims Objective Questions

items:
Q1. Which Article of the Indian Constitution confers inherent powers on the Supreme Court to pass any order necessary for doing 'complete justice' in any matter before it?
(a) Article 136
(b) Article 141
(c) Article 142
(d) Article 144
Correct Answer: (c) Article 142 [Explanation: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to issue any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, often utilized in landmark public interest cases.]

Q2. Under the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, which of the following Fundamental Rights CANNOT be suspended even during a National Emergency?
(a) Articles 14 and 19
(b) Articles 19 and 21
(c) Articles 20 and 21
(d) Articles 21 and 22
Correct Answer: (c) Articles 20 and 21 [Explanation: The 44th Amendment amended Article 359 to provide that the right to move any court for the enforcement of the rights conferred by Articles 20 (protection in respect of conviction) and 21 (right to life and personal liberty) cannot be suspended.]

Q3. The High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Amaravati was formally established on which date pursuant to the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014?
(a) June 2, 2014
(b) January 1, 2019
(c) August 15, 2019
(d) October 2, 2020
Correct Answer: (b) January 1, 2019 [Explanation: The separate High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Amaravati was constituted on January 1, 2019, following the Presidential Order issued under the provisions of the AP Reorganisation Act 2014.]

Q4. In which landmark case did the Supreme Court strike down the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act as unconstitutional?
(a) S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981)
(b) Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015)
(c) Common Cause v. Union of India (2018)
(d) Indira Jaising v. Supreme Court of India (2017)
Correct Answer: (b) Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) [Explanation: In the Fourth Judges Case (2015), a five-judge constitutional bench by 4:1 declared the 99th Constitutional Amendment and the NJAC Act unconstitutional, restoring the Collegium system.]

Q5. Which Article grants the President of India the power to consult the Supreme Court on questions of law or fact of public importance (Advisory Jurisdiction)?
(a) Article 129
(b) Article 131
(c) Article 143
(d) Article 145
Correct Answer: (c) Article 143 [Explanation: Under Article 143, the President may refer a question of law or fact to the Supreme Court for its advisory opinion.]
